newsitem.title: USA: U.S. current growth may not be sustainable--Parry.
newsitem.headline: U.S. current growth may not be sustainable--Parry.

text.p: The U.S. economy has been expanding at a healthy clip, but its current rate of growth might not be sustainable without sparking inflation in the long run, said the president of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco Robert Parry.

"The national economy has been performing extraordinary well ... We've had strong growth in output and employment combined with low inflation," Parry told an audience during a breakfast in Anchorage, Alaska on Monday.
A copy of Parry's speech was made available in New York by the San Francisco Fed.
Parry said the strength of the U.S. economy was broad-based, with the only sector bucking the trend being the U.S. federal government.
"It's important to note that this (economic) strength has been quite broad-based. In fact, the only exception is the federal government," Parry said.
He said strong spending in computers, consumer durables, structures and exports made those sectors stand out as the stars of the current expansion cycle.
Parry was quick to point out, however, that despite "all this strength, inflation remains quiescent."
He said the core Consumer Price Index -- which excludes food and energy price fluctuations -- rose a modest 2.5 percent over the past year, the lowest rate since 1966.
Parry also said the so-called "Misery Index" -- which is the sum of the current unemployment rate and the inflation rate -- is currently between the 7-1/2 and 8.0 percent range.
"It's not looking quite so miserable these days," he quipped.

The San Francisco Fed chief enumerated a couple of reasons why inflation has remained so low while the economy continued to grow at a brisk pace. Those factors included, among others, a strong dollar and workers' job insecurity.

Parry said, however, he believed most of the forces holding inflation down were temporary. He also said the current rate of economic growth was not likely to be sustainable without triggering inflation in the long run.

"Is this (economic) performance sustainable? I'm doubtful that it is. Specifically, if traditional relationships hold, we wouldn't expect the level of resource utilization ... to be sustainable without inflation becoming a problem," he said.
"The longer-run concern about inflation remains a live issue," the San Francisco Fed chief added.
Parry said price increases in some sectors have been held down by the rising exchange value of the dollar, but that phenomenon was likely to be temporary as well.
"This effect isn't likely to persist. We can't expect the dollar to continue to appreciate forever," he said.

Also, Parry said he was skeptical of arguments that the usage of modern technology was increasing productivity in the U.S. economy and, therefore, increasing the rate at which the economy can grow without spurring inflation.

"Powerful though these changes in productivity may be, I doubt strongly that they're enough to have raised our so-called potential growth from its recent rate of around 2.0 percent to a substantially higher rate," he said.
The San Francisco Fed president said, however, he believed the economy was likely to slow down from the torrid 5.8 percent growth rate seen in the first quarter.
"I'm reasonably optimistic that we will see some slowing to a more sustainable rate from the rapid growth in the first quarter," Parry said.
(( -- Jose Paulo Vicente, 212-859-1676 ))
